extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers of science, and advanced students of scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for judging the validity, strength, and application of inductive inferences in scientific inquiry — when a generalization from observed instances counts as a law or as reliable knowledge. Emphasizes distinctions among kinds of induction, the role of experience, and relations among laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction properly so called is Generalization from Experience: inferring from some individual instances in which a phenomenon is observed to occur, that it occurs in all instances of a certain class — namely, in all which resemble the former in the material circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induction consists in extending observed facts to unobserved cases that are sufficiently similar in their material circumstances; attention must be paid to which circumstances are 'material'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Invention (Colligation) and Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduction of a new conception (invention, colligation, explication of conceptions) is not the same as Induction: invention can aid description or hypothesis-formation but does not by itself constitute inductive proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate creating new conceptual frameworks (e.g., Kepler's ellipse) with induction; Kepler’s law supplied the minor premise in deductive proof rather than performing induction itself. Invention is an aid to discovery, not sufficient for inductive validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction/Description versus Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstraction (or colligation/description) extracts common characters from observations to represent phenomena, but such a general expression without inferring unknown facts is a Description, not an Induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when one is merely summarizing observed similarities (description) versus making an inductive leap to unobserved instances; the latter requires separate warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption of Parallel Cases (Uniformity of Nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every induction implies the assumption that there are parallel cases in nature — that what happens once will, under sufficient similarity of circumstances, happen again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assumed uniformity is a necessary condition for inductive conclusions; identifying appropriate notions of 'sufficient similarity' (material circumstances) is central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of Nature as an Inductive Generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposition that the course of nature is uniform is itself an induction — a generalization founded on prior generalizations — not an a priori principle that explains induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the uniformity axiom as a high-level induction supported by experience rather than as an independent philosophical justification for lower-level inductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductions as Syllogisms with Suppressed Major Premise
rubrics_metrics.description: Every induction can be cast into the form of a syllogism by supplying a major premise (ultimately the principle of the uniformity of nature), so inductive inference depends on such a general premise even if suppressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an inductive argument, make explicit its implicit major premise and test whether it is warranted by experience or by derivation from stronger inductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to Distinguish Material from Immaterial Circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction requires determining which circumstances are material (relevant to the phenomenon) and which are immaterial; valid generalization applies to instances that resemble in the material circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A key task in forming/assessing an induction is to identify the relevant conditions that must be shared across cases; failure to do so leads to erroneous generalizations (e.g., 'all swans are white').

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of Simple Enumeration (inductio per enumerationem simplicem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizing merely because no contradicting instance has been observed is insufficient for robust induction; simple enumeration is the form of unscientific induction and often inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple enumeration may be provisional or practically useful in absence of better methods, but scientific induction demands more searching investigation and tests (experiment/interrogation of nature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to Believe That Counterinstances Would Be Known
rubrics_metrics.description: Before concluding universality from observed uniformity, one must have reason to believe that, if counterinstances existed, we would have known of them; lacking that assurance, simple enumeration is weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether observational coverage and awareness are sufficient to rule out unknown exceptions — e.g., black swans were unknown to Europeans because of limited geographic exploration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stronger Inductions as Touchstone for Weaker Ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Stronger, better-established inductions serve as tests and supports for weaker ones; if a weaker induction can be deduced from stronger ones, it acquires their strength and becomes more certain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek connections that let you derive less-certain generalizations from well-established laws; binding a weak induction into a broader framework increases its credibility (example: Torricelli’s experiment deriving from three simpler laws).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict Resolution Among Inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: If an induction conflicts with stronger inductions or with deductive consequences of them, the weaker induction must be revised or abandoned unless the stronger induction’s scope has been overstated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use incompatibility among inductions to test and correct errors (e.g., astrology is abandoned when inconsistent with stronger scientific inductions about terrestrial causes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirmation via Ratiocination
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductions which can be connected by correct ratiocination (deductive links) are mutually confirmatory; derivation increases certainty and all linked inductions become more reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims, prefer those that fit into a network of deductions from established inductions; such interconnection raises overall confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of Nature as Simplest, Independent Uniformities
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature are those uniformities reduced to their simplest and fewest independent expressions from which more complex uniformities can be deduced; not every observed regularity counts as a law if it is derivable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In judging whether a generalization is a fundamental law, ask whether it is independent or simply a case/result of simpler laws (Kepler’s laws vs Newtonian laws example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation does not Replace Verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when a complex uniformity can be deduced from simpler laws, empirical verification by specific experience is still desirable and may be indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept deductive derivation alone as conclusive; seek empirical confirmation of deduced consequences (Torricelli example: although deducible, verification remains important).

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey of Existing Uniformities as Foundation for Inductive Method
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific formula of induction must rest on a survey of the types of uniformities already established by unscientific practice, to learn which classes of cases are more reliably uniform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before applying induction, examine what kinds of phenomena historically show stable uniformities (e.g., anatomy vs animal coloration) to calibrate expectations of reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Phenomena by Degree of Uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Different classes of phenomena exhibit different degrees of constancy; we may have greater warrant for universal claims in classes shown by experience to be highly invariable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate an inductive claim partly by placing the phenomenon in a class whose past uniformities are known (e.g., anatomical structure more constant than color).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of Experiment/Interrogation of Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific induction requires active interrogation of nature (experiment) rather than passive acceptance of presented facts; superior minds seek facts needed to reach safe conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer methods that actively seek disconfirming instances or control circumstances to isolate causal/material factors rather than relying on incidental observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Between Laws, Results of Laws, and Cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the hierarchy: some uniformities are fundamental laws, others are results or special cases that follow from these laws; proper scientific explanation seeks the fewest assumptions generating observed order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an assertion, analyze whether it is a primary law or a derivative case; favor explanations that reduce many phenomena to few simple principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility of Single-Instance Inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: In some cases, a single well-made observation or experiment may suffice for a universal induction when it falls within a class of phenomena governed by very strong, well-established regularities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the instance lies within a domain where existing knowledge confers high reliability (e.g., careful chemical analysis yielding a new substance may be taken as universal if methods trusted).
